samples.question: The top row of the picture is a hand of nine coloured discs, all nine colours different, standing side by side; the grey arrow under them shows that they are dealt one at a time in drawn left-to-right order. A thick black ring is drawn around the hand at one place: the ringed disc is the disc whose centre is nearest the centre of that ring, and the ring is drawn behind the discs, so a disc may cover part of it. In the middle of the picture is a row of coloured bins, all of different colours, and these are the piles: they receive discs in their drawn left-to-right order. Dealing goes round the bins in that order over and over, so the first disc of the hand goes to the leftmost bin, the next disc to the bin to its right, and so on; after the rightmost bin the next disc goes to the leftmost bin again, until all nine discs have been dealt. Each pile keeps its own discs in the order it received them, earliest received first. The bottom row of coloured chips is the pick-up order, read left to right as the grey arrow beneath it shows: each chip has the colour of one bin, every bin appears exactly once, and the piles are picked up in that order. The picked-up piles are then laid down end to end in one final row, each pile keeping its own order, earliest received first, so the first picked-up pile fills the leftmost places of the final row, the next picked-up pile the places just to its right, and so on. The nine places of the final row are numbered one to nine from the left. No pile and no final row is drawn anywhere in the picture; only the starting hand, the bins and the chips are drawn. Disc colours carry no rule and only name the discs. Once every disc has been dealt and every pile has been laid down, which numbered place of the final row holds the ringed disc? Answer with one word: one, two, three, four, five, six, seven, eight or nine.
